extracted.intended_audience: MER program developers, advisory committee members, NSF program officers, and mathematicians interested in mathematics education reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and indicators for evaluating the MER (Mathematics Education Reform) Forum's activities, workshops, advisory processes, dissemination, and impact on participants across K-12, undergraduate, and graduate levels. Includes participant survey metrics, meeting/productivity norms, and programmatic recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical style (lecture vs modeled pedagogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops were very lecture oriented; some participants wanted modeling of good classroom techniques and non-lecture teaching modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: breakout sessions that posed excellent questions for discussion or used videotapes to share teacher modeling; respondents noted presenters rarely exhibited good pedagogy in forum format. Recommendation: consider short presentation followed by structured discussion where participants grapple with real problems and see effective classroom pedagogy modeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency of format / use of limited time
rubrics_metrics.description: Many participants felt lecture-discussion style was perhaps the most efficient way to share information in the relatively short time frame of the workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off acknowledged: cooperative learning activities or non-lecture modes might not be efficient given time constraints. Suggested compromise: brief presentations plus structured discussions to both share information efficiently and model pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance willingness under cost/time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Likelihood of attendance depends on who pays expenses and participants' time availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: almost all would attend if all expenses paid; number drops to slightly less than half if they must pay their own transportation and conference fee; only 25-35% would/might attend if they had to pay all expenses. Note: time can be a more important resource than money for these busy participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived value of workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether participants indicate workshops were valuable experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: appreciation of opportunities to meet presenters/colleagues in informal settings; reports of learning new information; validation of participants' own educational notions and practices (e.g., 'helped solidify my confidence in my own teaching innovations').

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of information presented to participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether information presented is new to the target audience (mathematicians) even if not 'cutting edge' in math education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: much of the information (e.g., cooperative learning, teaching problem-solving skills) was not 'new' to math educators but was new to many mathematician participants; MER effectively brings educational ideas into the mathematics community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling reform-oriented pedagogy in breakout sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which workshop breakout sessions model non-traditional, reform-oriented pedagogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many participants desired more modeling in afternoon breakouts. Co-directors could encourage presenters to model reform-oriented pedagogy; complexity arises because mathematicians often prefer didactic approaches and want to maximize information in a 3-day workshop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory Committee member selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: How Advisory Committee members are chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members selected based on experience in education activities, leadership positions in the mathematics community, the K-12 mathematics community, and professional societies. Committee members bring their own perspectives rather than being charged with gathering information from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory Committee meeting productivity and time-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Productive use of scarce face-to-face time for the annual Advisory Committee meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting observed was short (1.5 hours) yet productive; much informal dialogue occurs outside formal meetings. Because members meet formally only once per year, limited face-to-face time should be spent as productively as possible; topics should be prioritized (e.g., departmental network, evaluation, future directions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissemination strategy (what/how to disseminate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about what MER should disseminate and how dissemination should occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee discussed using major organizations (AMS & MAA) to publicize MER ideas. Two network functions described: (1) push (push information onto readers via newsletters) and (2) pull (provide descriptions/statistics so readers can pull pertinent data). Choice of dissemination method depends on network intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Advisory Committee feedback to improve evaluation instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Soliciting and incorporating Advisory Committee input on survey instruments and other evaluation tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the meeting, the evaluation team solicited feedback and received constructive comments; instruments were improved because of their input. This is presented as good practice for instrument validity and stakeholder buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for systematic feedback channels to co-directors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether MER co-directors have a systematic avenue for gathering feedback from their constituency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern raised that in absence of systematic channels, co-directors must rely on questionable sources (most vocal people or chance encounters) for analyzing participant needs; implies criterion: establish systematic feedback mechanisms (surveys, structured input).

rubrics_metrics.name: Program focus alignment across education levels (K-12, undergraduate, graduate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether MER's structural supports and activities align with targeted educational levels (K-12, undergraduate, graduate) and intended outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate effectiveness MER specified criteria: (1) workshops or newsletters focused on these topics should exist; (2) participants should indicate they spend their time engaged in these educational initiatives; (3) participants should value MER's role in helping with their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop topic coverage (domains and trends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization and frequency analysis of workshop topics to trace organizational emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops categorized into domains: general issues, direct connections with K-12, university issues, general K-12 issues, and systemic issues. A matrix (Table 6) shows frequency trends; caveat: this is a rough estimate not accounting for session quality or length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant involvement measures (surveyed activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of participants' involvement in a range of educational activities (e.g., undergraduate curriculum reform, calculus reform, K-12 reform, programs for pre-service/in-service teachers, increasing participation of underrepresented groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used mailed survey with categorical responses (Not at all / A little / Considerably / Very). Results reported by role (mathematician vs math-educator) and by gender, and used to assess where MER participants are active and how MER relates to those activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on participants' work: facilitating communication and reducing isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which MER facilitates face-to-face interaction among mathematicians and reduces feelings of isolation in educational work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported outcomes: MER provided important function by facilitating communication, making participants feel less isolated, and validating educational work. Many attributed furthering their projects to connections made at MER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on participants' projects: providing methods, frameworks, and institutional leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether MER helps participants learn methods/materials, organize thinking, solve problems, and influence administrators/state policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: participants used others' ideas to expand efforts; Don Lewis talk provided conceptual framework applied later; MER membership helped members cite peer institutions to administrators and to expose state officials to reform ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for conducting educational research and program evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which MER supports members' involvement in educational research and their capacity to evaluate educational initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding: little interest among participants in conducting educational research; few sessions dealt with it; some participants struggled to evaluate programs outside their quantitative paradigms. Recommendation: MER consider offering sessions on methods for conducting educational evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource prioritization and cost-effectiveness (focus recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given limited resources, whether MER should concentrate efforts (e.g., on undergraduate education) rather than equally pushing less-popular areas (e.g., K-12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: concentrate on supporting undergraduate education where participant involvement is higher; alternative approaches include dedicating portions of undergraduate workshops to K-12 issues or creating special interest groups for less-popular pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration within and across professional communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which MER facilitates collaboration among mathematicians and between mathematicians and professional educators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: research mathematicians tended to form collaborations with other mathematicians or scientists rather than with professional educators. MER does not actively promote cross-community collaboration but does not oppose it; presence of notable math educators on Advisory Board suggests some interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of mathematics educators tied to mathematics ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived criterion that a mathematics educator's credibility within the mathematics community depends on demonstrated mathematics ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported culture: educational credibility for practitioners was often seen as contingent on meeting mathematics criteria; quotes illustrate that only when educators 'meet the mathematics criteria' do their educational ideas carry credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program reach: unique audience access
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether MER successfully reaches a unique subset of professionals (research-oriented mathematicians) not typically engaged by other education groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey comments: MER uniquely reaches university-level, research-oriented mathematicians to discuss teaching; this reach is presented as a distinctive and valuable measure of MER's role.
